account: The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) announced that on 25 February 2025 it began producing operational forecasts with AIFS Single, the deterministic version of its Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System. ECMWF runs it alongside its physics-based Integrated Forecasting System (IFS). ECMWF claimed tropical cyclone track gains of up to 20%. Pan and colleagues found that AIFS precipitation errors over China were lower than those of the IFS from April 2024 to March 2025, while AIFS underestimated extremes. On 1 July 2025 ECMWF launched the ensemble version, AIFS-ENS, operationally. The Science Operations Officer of the National Hurricane Center said that ECMWF's AI-driven global system was available for evaluation at the center during the 2025 season. ECMWF's evaluation of 2025 forecasts (8 May 2026) reports that AIFS errors were 5 to 15% lower than those of the IFS for most surface and upper-air variables. Cyclone position errors were substantially smaller, while cyclone intensity was under-predicted. No specific event in which AIFS beat the IFS is documented in the cited ECMWF sources. The Severe Event Catalogue page for Storm Eowyn states that wind gusts were not available for AIFS. In July 2026 a preprint partly written by ECMWF authors restated that machine-learning forecast models “tend to dramatically underestimate intensity” of tropical cyclones. The authors proposed a correction. Zhang and Ma found that the operational AIFS had a temperature error about 15.7% lower than the IFS control forecast in Inner Mongolia in summer 2026, while the IFS control forecast did better for heavy rain. The two studies by Chinese meteorological authors without ties to ECMWF confirm part of the ECMWF claim.

ai_role.statement: ECMWF's verification compares AIFS directly with the IFS. The only non-ECMWF cited source (NWS Q&A) confirms NHC evaluated ECMWF's AI system in 2025 but states no performance result. ECMWF is both the developer and the deployer, so its evaluations are the body reporting on its own system.

The authors work at the Shaanxi Meteorological Observatory, other Chinese weather services and Northwestern Polytechnical University, with no tie to ECMWF. They verified AIFS against 2,415 stations in China from 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025, a period that falls mostly before AIFS Single became operational.

The National Weather Service question-and-answer page states only that ECMWF's system was available for evaluation at the National Hurricane Center during the 2025 season.

fields.account: The European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) announced that on 25 February 2025 it began producing operational forecasts with AIFS Single, the deterministic version of its Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System. ECMWF runs it alongside its physics-based Integrated Forecasting System (IFS). ECMWF claimed tropical cyclone track gains of up to 20%. Pan and colleagues found that AIFS precipitation errors over China were lower than those of the IFS from April 2024 to March 2025, while AIFS underestimated extremes. On 1 July 2025 ECMWF launched the ensemble version, AIFS-ENS, operationally. The Science Operations Officer of the National Hurricane Center said that ECMWF's AI-driven global system was available for evaluation at the center during the 2025 season. ECMWF's evaluation of 2025 forecasts (8 May 2026) reports that AIFS errors were 5 to 15% lower than those of the IFS for most surface and upper-air variables. Cyclone position errors were substantially smaller, while cyclone intensity was under-predicted. No specific event in which AIFS beat the IFS is documented in the cited ECMWF sources. The Severe Event Catalogue page for Storm Eowyn states that wind gusts were not available for AIFS. In July 2026 a preprint partly written by ECMWF authors restated that machine-learning forecast models “tend to dramatically underestimate intensity” of tropical cyclones. The authors proposed a correction. Zhang and Ma found that the operational AIFS had a temperature error about 15.7% lower than the IFS control forecast in Inner Mongolia in summer 2026, while the IFS control forecast did better for heavy rain. The two studies by Chinese meteorological authors without ties to ECMWF confirm part of the ECMWF claim.
fields.summary: ECMWF's AIFS Single forecast model went into operation on 25 February 2025; ECMWF reports 5–15% lower errors than IFS, and two independent studies in China partly confirm the gain.

ratings.reason: No source reports a benefit to a named person, such as a decision changed by an AIFS forecast.

ECMWF reports errors 5 to 15% lower than the IFS for most variables in 2025, and an independent study in Inner Mongolia found a temperature error about 15.7% lower in summer 2026. That is a measured improvement in a forecasting capability, with weaker results for heavy rain, extremes and cyclone intensity.
The sources report forecast skill only; none documents a realized outcome for the public, such as a warning that worked better because of AIFS.
